readingHtml:
The City That Said Goodbye to Cars

A case study in urban transformation

A.In 2015, the mayor of Copenhagen stood in front of a crowded town hall and made a promise that many thought was impossible: within a decade, the city would become the first capital in the world to be carbon-neutral. At the time, Copenhagen was struggling with the same problems that face most growing cities — congested roads, rising pollution, and residents who complained that their neighbourhoods had become unlivable. Few believed the plan would work. Ten years later, the city has proved many of those sceptics wrong.

B.The idea was not new. As early as 2009, city planners had begun to discuss a bold strategy: to reduce the number of cars in the city centre and to make cycling, walking, and public transport the primary ways of getting around. What made Copenhagen’s plan different was not the goal, but the scale. Rather than gently discouraging drivers, the council made a series of decisions that changed the physical shape of the city. Parking spaces were removed. Whole streets were turned into pedestrian-only zones. A network of elevated cycle paths — the so-called “cycle super-highways” — was built to connect the suburbs with the city centre.

C.The cycling infrastructure is perhaps the most striking feature of the transformation. Copenhagen now has over 400 kilometres of dedicated cycle lanes, many of them separated from car traffic by curbs or planters. In winter, the snow is cleared from cycle paths before it is cleared from roads. At major intersections, cyclists are given priority with their own traffic lights. Perhaps most importantly, the city made a decision that no other capital had made: it began to measure its success not by how fast cars could move, but by how many people chose to cycle. Today, more than 60 per cent of Copenhagen residents commute to work or school by bike — a figure that would have seemed absurd a generation ago.

D.The transformation was not limited to transport. The city’s harbour, once an industrial area that residents avoided, has been cleaned and reopened as a public space. Old warehouses have been converted into apartments, restaurants, and cultural centres. A series of new bridges allow pedestrians and cyclists to cross the water easily. In summer, locals swim in the harbour — something that would have been unthinkable in the 1990s, when the water was considered unsafe. The city has also invested heavily in renewable energy, particularly wind power and district heating systems that use waste heat from factories.

E.Not everyone welcomed the changes. Small business owners in the city centre complained that removing parking spaces had reduced their customers. Some residents in the suburbs argued that the new cycle highways served wealthier neighbourhoods better than poorer ones. Critics noted that the transition had been expensive, and that the council had spent millions on projects that would take decades to pay back. Others pointed out that Copenhagen’s success was possible partly because the city was relatively small and wealthy — conditions that many other cities do not share.

F.Despite the criticisms, the results have been difficult to ignore. Air pollution in the city centre has dropped by more than 40 per cent since 2015. Traffic accidents involving cyclists have fallen, partly because of safer road design. Most importantly, surveys suggest that residents are happier with their city than they were a decade ago. Copenhagen has become a model that other cities now study carefully — from Paris to Bogotá to Seoul. The question is no longer whether a city can reduce its dependence on cars, but how quickly others will follow.
